A.explanation: Zero would be the resultant only if the rule were balanced in equilibrium, but the 4.0 N load moment is much larger than the opposing weight moment.

B.explanation: The clockwise $4.0 \text{ N} \times 0.40 \text{ m} = 1.6 \text{ N m}$ minus the anticlockwise $2.0 \text{ N} \times 0.10 \text{ m} = 0.20 \text{ N m}$ gives $1.4 \text{ N m}$ resultant.

C.explanation: This is the moment of the 4.0 N load alone about the 60 cm pivot and ignores the opposing $0.20 \text{ N m}$ moment due to the 2.0 N weight of the rule.

D.explanation: This adds the $1.6 \text{ N m}$ load moment and the $0.20 \text{ N m}$ weight moment instead of subtracting opposite clockwise and anticlockwise moments.

hints: Notice the pivot is at the 60 cm mark while the uniform rule's 2.0 N weight acts at the 50 cm centre and the 4.0 N load acts at the 100 cm end.
Recall moment = force x perpendicular distance, so convert the 40 cm load arm and the 10 cm weight arm to metres before multiplying.
Decide the sense of each moment about the pivot - load clockwise versus rule weight anticlockwise - then subtract to find the resultant magnitude.
walkthrough: Identify the two forces that have moments about the 60 cm pivot when horizontal: the 4.0 N load at the 100 cm end and the 2.0 N weight of the uniform rule at its 50 cm midpoint.
Calculate perpendicular distances: for the load $d = 100 - 60 = 40 \text{ cm} = 0.40 \text{ m}$ to the right, and for the rule $d = 60 - 50 = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.10 \text{ m}$ to the left.
Use $moment = F \times d$: load moment $= 4.0 \times 0.40 = 1.6 \text{ N m}$ clockwise, and weight moment $= 2.0 \times 0.10 = 0.20 \text{ N m}$ anticlockwise.
Take the resultant as clockwise minus anticlockwise: $1.6 - 0.20 = 1.4 \text{ N m}$.
